1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

Gold opened the sample at $273.90 (Aug 2000) and closed 2025 at $4325.60, compounding at 11.51% over ~25.3 years. The trajectory is not linear: four distinct macro phases are visible.

  • 2000–2011 Secular Bull: A multi-year rally driven by dollar weakness, emerging-market demand, and post-crisis safe-haven flows. The peak of $1,888.70 was reached on 22 Aug 2011.
  • 2011–2015 Bear Market: A prolonged correction as real rates rose and risk appetite recovered. The trough of $1,050.80 on 17 Dec 2015 marked a –44.4% drawdown — the deepest in the sample.
  • 2016–2019 Consolidation: Range-bound behavior between ~$1,050 and $1,550 as the Fed normalized policy.
  • 2020–2025 New Bull: Post-COVID monetary expansion, geopolitical stress, and later central-bank buying pushed gold to successive all-time highs, ending 2025 above $4,300.
Regime shading: Low-Vol (blue), Normal (grey), High-Vol (orange), Crisis (red). Shading is based on 30-day rolling volatility and concurrent return direction.

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility clustering is pronounced. A Ljung–Box test on squared daily returns yields LB(1) = 114.9 (p < 0.001), confirming that large moves tend to follow large moves — a hallmark of macro assets.

We classify regimes using 30-day rolling volatility percentiles:

  • Low-Vol: < 13.0% annualized — calm trending periods.
  • Normal: 13.0%–16.9% — typical market conditions.
  • High-Vol: > 16.9% with positive drift — volatile but not collapsing.
  • Crisis: > 16.9% with negative drift — stress episodes.

3. Seasonal & Calendar-Based Patterns

We test monthly and day-of-week effects using one-way ANOVA on aggregated log returns.

  • Monthly seasonality: F = 0.82, p = 0.620 → not statistically significant at conventional levels. Observed differences are likely noise.
  • Day-of-week seasonality: F = 0.97, p = 0.424 → not statistically significant.

That said, the point estimates show January and August as the strongest months on average, while June is the weakest. Analysts should treat any month-trading strategy with caution given the high variance.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

Gold’s daily return distribution deviates sharply from normality:

  • Skewness: -0.317 (moderate left skew — large negative days are more common than large positive days).
  • Excess Kurtosis: 5.17 (fat tails — extreme moves are far more likely than under a normal model).
  • Jarque–Bera test: p < 0.001 → reject normality.

Value-at-Risk (historical):

  • 5% daily VaR = -1.76%
  • 1% daily VaR = -3.10%
Risk management implication: A normal model would materially understate tail risk. Stress-testing and non-parametric VaR are preferred for gold allocations.

5. Momentum Dynamics & Liquidity Behavior

Moving-average crossovers (50/200-day) capture medium-term trend shifts. Golden crosses have historically preceded multi-year rallies; death crosses have coincided with corrections or extended bear phases.

Volume insights (post-2004, where data is reliable):

  • Average volume on down days (5,195) is ~20% higher than on up days (4,333), suggesting loss-aversion-driven selling pressure.
  • Correlation between volume and absolute return is weak and slightly negative (r = -0.029), indicating volume does not scale linearly with price shocks.
  • Early-year volume (2000–2003) is frequently zero or near-zero and should be disregarded for liquidity analysis.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

  • Long-term compounding is strong but lumpy. Gold’s ~11.5% annualized return over 25 years masks multi-year drawdowns exceeding 40%. Position sizing must account for regime persistence.
  • Volatility regimes are sticky. Crisis states do not resolve overnight; risk models should use regime-switching rather than single-state volatility assumptions.
  • Seasonal edges are statistically weak. Do not overweight calendar-based tactical trades without additional confirming signals.
  • Tail risk is real and non-normal. Daily 1% VaR of ~–3.1% and excess kurtosis >5 imply that standard mean–variance optimization will understate portfolio risk.
  • Current context (late 2025): Gold is in a strong uptrend with elevated but not crisis-level volatility. The 2024–2025 rally (~64% log return in 2025 alone) has pushed price to unprecedented levels; mean-reversion risk is rising even as macro drivers (de-dollarization, geopolitical hedging) remain supportive.
Bottom line for allocation: Gold remains a robust diversifier with positive skew over long horizons, but its path is characterized by deep, persistent drawdowns and fat-tailed daily moves. Size positions to survive Crisis regimes, not just Low-Vol trends.
